newsitem.title: COMOROS: Indian Ocean "paradise" no stranger to tragedy.
newsitem.headline: Indian Ocean "paradise" no stranger to tragedy.

text.p: Tourists in the idyllic Indian Ocean Comoro Islands woke up on Sunday to find mangled bodies washing ashore on palm-fringed beaches.
But the crash of a hijacked Ethiopian Airlines plane in the sea only a few hundred metres (yards) offshore from the main Grand Comore island is only the latest tragedy to hit the tropical "paradise".

Coups, assassinations, mercenaries -- the tiny chain of four volcanic islands in the Mozambique channel 300 km (190 miles) northwest of Madagascar and 300 km east of the African continent has seen them all.

Twenty years of civil strife include 17 coups and coup attempts, the assassination of a president, an invasion by South African-backed mercenaries, and frequent "interventions" by France -- the former colonial power.
The presence of the mercenaries led by the veteran French adventurer Bob Denard made them infamous and they were dubbed the "Soldier of Fortune Islands".

Denard's motley band of followers grew rich on the profits of sanctions-busting on behalf of apartheid South Africa. In those years it was also one of the few destinations to which South Africans could travel without problems.
South African companies still run most of the best hotels on the islands -- a dream location for water sports fans.
Denard was at the heart of at least three coups on the islands, the last of which was quashed by French troops in October 1995.
That attempt led to fresh elections that brought to power the current president, Mohamed Taki, a devout Moslem.
Taki flirted with Iran and banned the sale of alcohol -- except to diplomats and in hotels.

Last May he criticised women for wearing miniskirts and short dresses, sparking fears he wanted to set the Comoros, which depend totally on tourism for foreign exchange, on an Islamic fundamentalist path.
In 1975, after the islands became independent from France, Denard -- leading a group of white mercenaries known as Les Affreux (The Terrible Ones) -- helped overthrow then-President Ahmed Abdallah.
History turned full circle three years later when he restored Abdallah to power in an invasion in which Abdallah's predecessor, Ali Soilih, was killed "trying to escape".
Abdallah himself was killed in 1989. Denard was present in the same room though he denies any connection with the death.
One of the poorest nations in the world, the Comoros have few natural resources, a chronic shortage of arable land, and a high population density.
Most people are subsistence farmers but the islands are unable to feed themselves and rely on rice imports.
There is small-scale fishing but this barely satisfies local demand and per capita income hovers at about $410 a year.

There are four main inhabited islands -- Grande Comore, Ajouan, Moheli and Mayotte. The Comoros, with a population of 510,000, are mountainous but their natural forest cover has been largely denuded by cultivation.
